issues.claim: The station opened in 1877 as Shaftesbury Road.
issues.correct: Opened 1 April 1873 as Shaftesbury Road (L&SWR); renamed Ravenscourt Park on 1 March 1888. Corbett renamed the house in 1747, consistent with '18th century'.
issues.suggested_text: In the 18th century the owner, Thomas Corbett, renamed his house Ravenscourt; ravens were on his coat of arms. The grounds became a public park. The station opened in 1873 as Shaftesbury Road.

issues.problem: Wrong year for the current hornbeam ring.
issues.correct: The current hornbeams were planted in 1997, in a ceremony led by five families of seven sisters.
issues.suggested_text: By local tradition they were planted by seven sisters. The first trees were elms; the ring has been replanted several times, most recently with hornbeams in 1997.

issues.claim: The station opened in 1856 as Snaresbrook & Wanstead.
issues.correct: Opened 22 August 1856 as Snaresbrook; became 'Snaresbrook for Wanstead' in 1857 and 'Snaresbrook and Wanstead' in 1898; back to plain Snaresbrook in 1947 when it joined the Central line. Also, Wikipedia gives the Sayers Brook origin without a hedge, while Londonist says 'supposedly', so the hedged head is fine.
issues.suggested_text: It may be a changed form of 'Sayers Brook', a small stream flowing into the River Roding. The station opened in 1856 and was called Snaresbrook and Wanstead for many years.

issues.claim: The station opened on the Central line in 1948.
issues.problem: Reads as if the station first opened in 1948. It opened in 1934 as a main-line station; Central line trains started in 1948.
issues.correct: Opened 9 July 1934 (Great Western and Great Central Joint Railway); Central line services from 21 November 1948.
issues.suggested_text: The leap was probably a narrow crossing on the River Pinn. 'Gardens' was used for new suburban housing. The station opened in 1934; Central line trains came in 1948.

issues.claim: Pinner Fair has been held every year since a charter of 1336.
issues.problem: Not every year: the fair was cancelled in 2020 and 2021 because of COVID-19.
issues.correct: Charter granted by Edward III in 1336; fair held annually since, except 2020 and 2021.
issues.suggested_text: It ends in Old English ora, a slope or hill; the River Pinn was later named after the village. Pinner Fair has been held almost every year since a charter of 1336.

issues.claim: The road ran through land belonging to the church.
issues.problem: Could not confirm. Hidden London supports the head (the name refers to St Mary's rectory, Stoke Newington), but says the road was renamed when builders replaced market gardens on part of Shacklewell Lane, and that it led towards the rectory. It does not say the land belonged to the church. Wikipedia station and Stoke Newington pages say nothing on the name; a web search found nothing more.
issues.correct: Hidden London: the name refers to the rectory of St Mary's, Stoke Newington, which the road led towards via Church Street. Station opened 1872. 'New farm by the tree stumps' for Stoke Newington matches Mills (stocc + niwe tun).
issues.suggested_text: The road led towards St Mary's rectory, via Stoke Newington Church Street. Stoke Newington means the new farm by the tree stumps.

issues.problem: Sources disagree on the year: Wikipedia (Redbridge, London) says 1921, Londonist says 1922. Other facts check out (17th-century record per Londonist, station opened 14 Dec 1947, borough 1965).
issues.suggested_text: The bridge was recorded from the 17th century and demolished in the early 1920s. The station, opened in 1947, had the name before the London Borough of Redbridge, created in 1965.
